recommendations.trigger: The PVT-B or typing shows a deviation from your personal baseline (e.g. 1/RT below threshold), even if you feel rested
recommendations.action: Don't rely on how you feel: repeat the 3-minute PVT-B before any critical task and, if possible, postpone the task until your results are back to normal.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: Van Dongen HPA, Maislin G, Mullington JM, Dinges DF. (2003). The cumulative cost of additional wakefulness: dose-response effects on neurobehavioral functions and sleep physiology from chronic sleep restriction and total sleep deprivation. Sleep 26(2):117-126. Erratum: Sleep 2004;27(4):600. + NASA Evidence Report 2016 (Chronic Sleep Loss section)

steps: Take the 3-minute reaction test.
Postpone critical tasks by 2 hours, if possible.

recommendations.trigger: A sustained deviation (several sessions) after short nights
recommendations.action: Prioritise a longer sleep opportunity (sleep extension/recovery) over the next nights; a single recovery night may not be enough.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: Flynn-Evans E, Gregory K, Arsintescu L, Whitmire A. (2016). Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload. NASA Human Research Program, Behavioral Health and Performance Element (Approved for Public Release: April 11, 2016). (Banks et al.: dose-dependent recovery; one night is not enough)

steps: Go to bed an hour earlier for the next 3 nights.
Keep your sleep window free of work and screens.
Take the reaction test again after the second night.

recommendations.trigger: Sleepiness or a deviation during the day, with a window for a break
recommendations.action: If you take a nap, keep it short (~10 minutes) and don't start critical tasks right after waking; a 30-minute nap impaired performance for up to an hour (sleep inertia). Schedule naps deliberately, so they don't disrupt your circadian rhythm.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: Flynn-Evans E, Gregory K, Arsintescu L, Whitmire A. (2016). Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload. NASA Human Research Program, Behavioral Health and Performance Element (Approved for Public Release: April 11, 2016). (Hilditch et al. 2016; Mars-520 observations on napping)

steps: Keep any nap to about 10 minutes.
Wait 30 minutes after waking before a critical task.
Log the nap in the app.

recommendations.trigger: Slower response speed before a task that demands high vigilance
recommendations.action: Time your caffeine around the task and keep it away from bedtime: astronauts who used stimulants reported falling asleep with more difficulty.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: Flynn-Evans E, Gregory K, Arsintescu L, Whitmire A. (2016). Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload. NASA Human Research Program, Behavioral Health and Performance Element (Approved for Public Release: April 11, 2016). (Wyatt et al. 2004; Whitmire et al. 2013)

steps: Have your caffeine before the task, not after it.
Skip caffeine in the 6 hours before bedtime.
Take the reaction test before you start the task.

recommendations.trigger: Deviations at unusual hours / after schedule changes (a sign of circadian misalignment)
recommendations.action: Follow the station's lighting schedule (LED/SSLA, which simulates the light–dark cycle) and fixed sleep times; use the time set aside for relaxation and self-care.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: NASA HFBP. Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules (NASA reference page). + NASA Evidence Report 2016 (SSLA)

steps: Follow the station's lighting schedule today.
Go to bed and get up at your scheduled times.
Use your scheduled relaxation time.

recommendations.trigger: Typing/PVT deviations together with low mood or social withdrawal
recommendations.action: Use the self-care strategies NASA recommends: a regular journal, virtual contact with family, activities that break the monotony (e.g. tending plants, looking out of the window).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Leading to In-mission Health and Performance and Long-term Health Effects

source.citation: NASA HFBP. Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders (NASA reference page).

steps: Write a short journal entry today.
Book a call with your family.
Spend 15 minutes on something you enjoy.

recommendations.trigger: A PVT-B deviation beyond the derived threshold (≥~1.24 SD from baseline on 1/RT or lapses) over several sessions or days, or before a critical operation (a design threshold, not a published one)
recommendations.action: Notify the crew medical officer (CMO): they assess sleep, workload and any sleep or alertness aids already in use. Sleep aids are the most used countermeasure on the ISS, and their effect on sleep inertia after a forced awakening is still being studied.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: Flynn-Evans E, Gregory K, Arsintescu L, Whitmire A. (2016). Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload. NASA Human Research Program, Behavioral Health and Performance Element (Approved for Public Release: April 11, 2016). (Executive summary: countermeasures; sleep inertia with hypnotics)

steps: Send your typing and reaction results to the medical officer.
Note your recent sleep and workload.
Tell the medical officer about any sleep aids you use.

recommendations.trigger: Persistent behavioural deviations (typing + PVT) together with changes in mood, sleep or behaviour reported by the astronaut or the crew
recommendations.action: The CMO carries out a structured assessment and documents it; behavioural symptoms that go undetected or are poorly managed can progress to psychiatric disorders.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Leading to In-mission Health and Performance and Long-term Health Effects

source.citation: NASA Human Research Roadmap. Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Leading to In-mission Health and Performance and Long-term Health Effects (Short Title: Behavioral Health). Last Published 05/13/25. (Risk Statement and HSRB State of Knowledge)

steps: Book a private session with the medical officer.
Note any changes in mood, sleep or behaviour.
Share your typing and reaction results.

recommendations.trigger: The deviation persists despite level 1–2 countermeasures, or appears in several crew members (suspected overload or scheduling problems)
recommendations.action: Ask Earth to replan the schedule (lighter workload, protected sleep windows); the HRR documents overload and scheduling problems in flight.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload

source.citation: NASA Human Research Roadmap. Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload (Short Title: Sleep). Last Published 05/13/25. (HSRB State of Knowledge)

steps: Send your sleep and workload data to Earth.
Ask for a lighter schedule and protected sleep windows.
Follow the revised schedule when it arrives.

recommendations.trigger: Behavioural or psychological signs that do not improve on board
recommendations.action: Set up a private conference with medical and behavioural health professionals on Earth; on distant missions, allow for the communication delay (up to 42 min on deep-space missions, according to the NASA presentation by Beard et al. 2021) and send the data package in advance.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders Leading to In-mission Health and Performance and Long-term Health Effects

source.citation: NASA HFBP. Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders (NASA reference page). + Beard BL, Russell B, Krihak M, Burian B, Noel J, Beaugrand D, Shaw T, Pletcher D, Martin K. (2021). Supporting Crew Medical Decisions on Deep Space Missions: Real-Time Performance Monitoring. Presentation, 11th IAASS Conference 2021 (virtual). NASA NTRS 20210022711.

steps: Request a private conference with Earth.
Send your data package ahead of the call.
Keep up level 1 self-care while you wait for the reply.

recommendations.trigger: Daily in flight, especially if your heart rate at a standardised submaximal workload rises >3% above your personal average or your fitness score drops.
recommendations.action: Follow the daily aerobic and resistance exercise prescription (~1.5 h/day, 6–7 days/week) and include the prescribed high-intensity sessions; repeat the standardised submaximal test under the same conditions.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

source.citation: NASA HRP, fitness risk page; Moore et al. 2014 (via Fitness Evidence Report p.34); CV Evidence Report p.30–31 (English 2020)

steps: Do today's full aerobic and resistance session.
Include the prescribed high-intensity intervals.
Repeat the submaximal test under the same conditions.
recommendations.note: Vigorous exercise was associated with a smaller drop in VO2peak (CV ER: −6% vs −15%), but the Fitness ER reports −7%/−10% for the same study.

recommendations.trigger: At check-in: in-flight systolic pressure up to ~14 mmHg below the pre-flight baseline, with no symptoms.
recommendations.action: No action needed: it is the expected adaptation to microgravity. Record the value; the app compares it with your in-flight baseline, not the one from Earth.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: Norsk P et al. 2015 J Physiol 593:573-584; Fu Q et al. 2019 Circulation 140:729-738

steps: Record the value at check-in.
No other action needed.
recommendations.note: The figures are confirmed only in the abstract.

recommendations.trigger: In the last 12–20 h before landing / the return to gravity.
recommendations.action: Follow the prescribed fluid and salt loading protocol (e.g. 18–20 ml/kg saline solution, 3–4 times with meals) and put on the compression garments (Kentavr/AGS/graded compression) as instructed.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: CV Evidence Report (2022) p.31–35 PDF; Lee SMC et al. 2020 Front Physiol 11:784; NASA CV Risk page ('Lower-body compression garments and drinking lots of fluids prior to landing')

steps: Follow the fluid and salt loading protocol.
Put on your compression garments as instructed.
Tell the medical officer if you feel unwell.
recommendations.note: The effect of fluid loading on plasma volume has not been shown directly after long missions (CV ER p.32).

recommendations.trigger: In the first hours to days after landing (or after descending to the Moon/Mars), at any dizziness on standing.
recommendations.action: Avoid activities that cause orthostatic hypotension (standing up suddenly, standing still for a long time), keep the compression on, and sit or lie down at once if you feel dizzy; do the app's stand test only with a crewmate present.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: CV Evidence Report (2022) p.26 PDF ('flight surgeons guide astronauts to avoid activities that may provoke the onset of orthostatic hypotension'); Lee SMC et al. 2015 Aerosp Med Hum Perform 86:A54-A67

steps: Stand up slowly, in stages.
Keep your compression garments on.
Sit or lie down at once if you feel dizzy.
Do the stand test only with a crewmate present.
recommendations.note: The 'test only with a crewmate present' rule is a safety choice of the prototype.

recommendations.trigger: Before every heart rate, HRV or blood pressure check-in.
recommendations.action: Measure under the same conditions (same time, same position, after 5 minutes of rest, before exercise) so that deviations from the baseline can be interpreted.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: Buchheit M 2014 Front Physiol 5:73 (individual interpretation accounting for measurement error and SWC; 5-min resting recordings)

steps: Measure at the same time each day.
Rest for 5 minutes beforehand, in the same position.
Measure before exercise.
recommendations.note: The source comes from sports medicine, not spaceflight.

recommendations.trigger: Resting heart rate with a 7-day mean > baseline + 1×individual CV for ≥3 days, or lnRMSSD < baseline − 0.5×CV, TOGETHER with symptoms (palpitations, dizziness, unusual tiredness).
recommendations.action: Notify the crew medical officer (CMO) for a re-assessment (repeat measurement, ECG if available) and a private medical conference with the flight surgeon.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: CV Evidence Report (2022) p.79 PDF (at least two ISS crew members have extra medical training for less urgent problems, supported by the flight surgeon); Buchheit 2014 for the threshold logic

steps: Measure your heart rate and blood pressure again.
Note any symptoms in the app.
Send the chart to the medical officer.
recommendations.note: The numerical escalation threshold is not published for astronauts; the CMO's role is verified.

recommendations.trigger: New swelling, pain or a feeling of pressure in the neck (especially on the left), a new one-sided headache, or facial swelling beyond the usual in-flight puffiness.
recommendations.action: Notify the CMO, who contacts the doctors on Earth for a guided ultrasound of the jugular vein (stagnant flow was found in 6/11 and an occlusive clot was treated on board).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: NASA HSRB CV Risk – Concern of Venous Thromboembolism; CV Evidence Report (2022) p.19–21 PDF (Marshall-Goebel 2019; Pavela 2022)

steps: Tell the medical officer today.
Note where it hurts and since when.
Avoid straining until you are assessed.
recommendations.note: The flow and thrombosis data are verified; the list of trigger symptoms is derived (the clot described had no symptoms, so symptoms may be absent).

recommendations.trigger: On the stand test after returning to gravity: a drop in SBP ≥20 mmHg or DBP ≥10 mmHg within 3 min, or a heart rate rise ≥30 bpm from the supine value, or presyncope.
recommendations.action: Stop the test, lie down and notify the CMO / flight surgeon; do not resume standing activity until you have been assessed.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: Freeman R et al. 2011 Clin Auton Res 21:69-72 (consensus criteria – text not read); CV Evidence Report p.25–26 PDF (incidence of presyncope)

steps: Stop the test and lie down.
Notify the medical officer.
Stay off your feet until you are assessed.
recommendations.note: The numerical criteria still need to be confirmed against the consensus text.

recommendations.trigger: Syncope (loss of consciousness), sustained palpitations or an irregular rhythm, chest pain, or suspected venous thrombosis.
recommendations.action: The CMO starts the emergency response and immediately contacts the flight surgeon on Earth (in low Earth orbit: a ~2-s delay, return to Earth possible); on missions to Mars the crew must be able to stabilise the situation on their own.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: CV Evidence Report (2022) p.79 PDF (Distance from Earth); p.13 PDF (a 14-beat episode of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia); NASA CV Risk page (arrhythmias, clots)

steps: Lie down and call a crewmate.
Alert the medical officer at once.
The medical officer contacts the flight surgeon on Earth.
recommendations.note: Not a NASA medical protocol; the prototype only recommends escalating.

recommendations.trigger: A loss of aerobic fitness >20% vs before flight on the periodic test, or a rising heart rate at submaximal effort despite following the prescription.
recommendations.action: Send the data to the exercise specialists on Earth so they can review the prescription (intensity, volume).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

source.citation: NASA HRP, fitness risk page (periodic self-assessments used to optimise training; 12–38% lose >20%)

steps: Send your fitness test results to Earth.
Keep following the current prescription until you get an answer.
recommendations.note: The 20% threshold is a NASA descriptive category, not a published operational criterion.

recommendations.trigger: Before landing after a long mission, for astronauts at higher risk (women, previous presyncope, low supine blood pressure/DBP vs baseline).
recommendations.action: The team on Earth plans the landing day: reduced activities, medical support and extended recovery.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Cardiovascular Adaptations Contributing to Adverse Mission Performance and Health Outcomes

source.citation: Lee SMC et al. 2015 Aerosp Med Hum Perform 86(12 Suppl):A54-A67 (conclusion: planners and physicians should anticipate adapting activities and medical support); CV Evidence Report p.24–28 PDF

steps: Review the landing-day plan with the medical officer.
Follow the fluid and compression protocol.
Plan for help on the first day back.
recommendations.note: The individual risk factors come from small studies (Waters 2002, Charles 1999).

recommendations.trigger: Yellow alert: your mean night-time heart rate is +3 bpm above your personal median, or a single night is ≥ +4 bpm (a NightSignal threshold; using it as level 1 is a SHADOW choice).
recommendations.action: Fill in the short context journal in the app: symptoms (cough, fever, headache, tiredness), short sleep, stress, hard exercise. Measure again the next night. In the study, alerts were also triggered by stress or other events unrelated to infection, and participants annotated their alerts through questionnaires.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Alavi A, Bogu GK, Wang M, Rangan ES, Brooks AW, et al., Snyder MP. 2022. Real-time alerting system for COVID-19 and other stress events using wearable data. Nature Medicine 28:175–184.

steps: Fill in the short symptom journal.
Go to bed an hour earlier tonight.
Measure again the next night.

recommendations.trigger: Any active immune alert, or sleep below your personal baseline.
recommendations.action: Prioritise sleep and fatigue management according to the schedule (sleep and circadian rhythm are directly linked to immune function; in orbit, sleep is shorter and rhythms are misaligned). Use the behavioural and fatigue support services available.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Crucian BE, Choukèr A, Simpson RJ, Mehta S, Marshall G, Smith SM, et al., Sams C. 2018. Immune System Dysregulation During Spaceflight: Potential Countermeasures for Deep Space Exploration Missions. Frontiers in Immunology 9:1437.

steps: Go to bed an hour earlier tonight.
Keep your sleep window free of work.
Use the fatigue support services if you need them.

recommendations.trigger: Always, as prevention (not only during an alert).
recommendations.action: Follow the prescribed aerobic and resistance exercise programme. In the HRP Evidence Report, better pre-flight fitness was associated with a lower risk of viral reactivation (29–39%), and the candidate countermeasure regime includes aerobic and resistance exercise, diet, supplements and VR exercises to reduce stress.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Mehta S, Crucian B. 2022. Evidence Report: Risk of Crew Adverse Health Event Due to Altered Immune Response. NASA Human Research Program, Human Health Countermeasures Element, Johnson Space Center (Approved for Public Release June 1, 2022).

steps: Do today's aerobic and resistance session.
Use a stress-reduction session if one is scheduled.

recommendations.trigger: Daily, especially in the first month of the mission (the period with the most notable events).
recommendations.action: A quick self-check of your skin and lips (rashes, irritated redness, cold sores) and of upper respiratory symptoms; record them in the app. Rashes were the most reported event on the ISS (1.12 per flight year).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Crucian B, Babiak-Vazquez A, Johnston S, Pierson DL, Ott CM, Sams C. 2016. Incidence of clinical symptoms during long-duration orbital spaceflight. International Journal of General Medicine 9:383–391.

steps: Check your skin and lips for rashes or sores.
Note any cough, sore throat or runny nose.
Record what you find in the app.

recommendations.trigger: Permanent.
recommendations.action: Stick to the prescribed menu and nutritional supplementation. Crucian 2018 discusses nutrition and functional foods as an immune countermeasure (the ISS menu is low in fruit and vegetables).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Crucian BE, Choukèr A, Simpson RJ, Mehta S, Marshall G, Smith SM, et al., Sams C. 2018. Immune System Dysregulation During Spaceflight: Potential Countermeasures for Deep Space Exploration Missions. Frontiers in Immunology 9:1437.

steps: Eat the meals on your menu.
Take your scheduled nutritional supplements.

recommendations.trigger: NightSignal red alert: mean night-time heart rate ≥ +4 bpm above your personal median two nights in a row, especially if skin temperature exceeds the derived SHADOW threshold or symptoms appear.
recommendations.action: Notify the crew medical officer (CMO) with the heart rate and temperature chart against your baseline and your symptom journal. Only the CMO decides on assessment or treatment; the app does not recommend medicines.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Alavi A, Bogu GK, Wang M, Rangan ES, Brooks AW, et al., Snyder MP. 2022. Real-time alerting system for COVID-19 and other stress events using wearable data. Nature Medicine 28:175–184.

steps: Go to bed an hour earlier for the next 3 nights.
Take your temperature morning and evening.
Fill in the symptom journal (cough, headache, tiredness).

recommendations.trigger: A skin rash, cold sore (possible HSV-1/VZV reactivation), or allergic or upper respiratory symptoms that appeared during the mission.
recommendations.action: Report to the CMO and describe where it is and how it is changing. Herpes reactivation is usually without symptoms, but sometimes produces lesions with infectious virus, so it matters for the other crew members too.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Rooney BV, Crucian BE, Pierson DL, Laudenslager ML, Mehta SK. 2019. Herpes Virus Reactivation in Astronauts During Spaceflight and Its Application on Earth. Frontiers in Microbiology 10:16.

steps: Tell the medical officer today.
Note where it is and how it has changed.
Avoid close contact if you have a cold sore.

recommendations.trigger: A “notable” event by NASA's definition: the symptom lasts >1 week, recurs or worsens, or does not respond to treatment.
recommendations.action: The CMO passes the case to the flight surgeons on Earth, with the data series against the baseline. On missions with a communication delay, the data package is sent asynchronously.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Mehta S, Crucian B. 2022. Evidence Report: Risk of Crew Adverse Health Event Due to Altered Immune Response. NASA Human Research Program, Human Health Countermeasures Element, Johnson Space Center (Approved for Public Release June 1, 2022).

steps: Keep filling in your symptom journal daily.
The medical officer sends your case to Earth.

recommendations.trigger: Repeated red alerts (a cluster of ≥2 consecutive red days) that do not resolve, or combined with persistent fever or symptoms (escalation proposed by SHADOW).
recommendations.action: Escalate to the medical team on the ground for assessment and possible biological samples (saliva, blood or urine for viral and immune markers, following the HRP research direction).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: NASA. Risk of Altered Immune System Responses (NASA HRP risk page; page last updated May 16, 2025).

steps: Keep measuring your temperature twice a day.
Collect samples if Earth asks for them.
Follow the guidance from the ground.

recommendations.trigger: After landing: up to ~30 days after the ISS (documented VZV/CMV shedding).
recommendations.action: The medical team on the ground should be informed about the risk of passing shed viruses to newborns, seronegative adults or immunocompromised people around the astronaut.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of In Mission Impacts, Adverse Health Events or Long-Term Health Impacts due to Altered Immune Response

source.citation: Rooney BV, Crucian BE, Pierson DL, Laudenslager ML, Mehta SK. 2019. Herpes Virus Reactivation in Astronauts During Spaceflight and Its Application on Earth. Frontiers in Microbiology 10:16.

steps: Follow the post-landing contact guidance.
Tell your family about the precautions.

recommendations.trigger: Daily exercise volume or load (resistance + aerobic) below your personal plan, or any day without exercise
recommendations.action: Complete the prescription: ~1.5 h/day of resistance and aerobic exercise, 6–7 days/week, with a focus on loaded exercises for the lower limbs (ARED).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

source.citation: NASA HRP (2025). Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness (official page, updated 16 May 2025)

steps: Complete today's resistance and aerobic session.
Focus on loaded leg exercises on ARED.
Log the session in the app.

recommendations.trigger: The load used on ARED is below the load in your personal baseline
recommendations.action: Raise the load gradually towards the pre-flight level. ARED allows up to 600 lbf (1675 N), and heavy loading together with adequate nutrition preserved hip BMD in the Smith 2012 study (n=5).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone

source.citation: Smith SM, Heer MA, Shackelford LC, Sibonga JD, Ploutz-Snyder L, Zwart SR (2012). Benefits for bone from resistance exercise and nutrition in long-duration spaceflight: Evidence from biochemistry and densitometry. J Bone Miner Res 27(9):1896-1906

steps: Raise your ARED load by one step.
Log the new load in the app.

recommendations.trigger: Body mass is falling from your personal baseline, or energy intake is below plan
recommendations.action: Stick to the energy intake and the vitamin D supplement in your plan. ARED's benefit for bone was seen together with maintained body mass and nominal vitamin D.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone

source.citation: Smith SM, Heer MA, Shackelford LC, Sibonga JD, Ploutz-Snyder L, Zwart SR (2012). Benefits for bone from resistance exercise and nutrition in long-duration spaceflight: Evidence from biochemistry and densitometry. J Bone Miner Res 27(9):1896-1906

steps: Eat every meal on your plan.
Take your vitamin D supplement.
Weigh yourself at the next scheduled check.

recommendations.trigger: Planning the day's loading sessions (impact/resistance)
recommendations.action: If the schedule allows, split the loading into 2–4 shorter sessions a few hours apart, instead of one long one. Note: the evidence comes ONLY from rat studies (Robling 2000–2002) and it is not a NASA procedure.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone

source.citation: Robling AG, Hinant FM, Burr DB, Turner CH (2002). Improved bone structure and strength after long-term mechanical loading is greatest if loading is separated into short bouts. J Bone Miner Res 17(8):1545-1554

steps: Split today's loading into 2–4 short sessions.
Leave a few hours between sessions.

recommendations.trigger: The periodic fitness test is missing or overdue
recommendations.action: Do the periodic fitness self-assessment (strength/endurance) to update the deviation from your baseline.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

source.citation: NASA HRP (2025). Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness (official page, updated 16 May 2025)

steps: Do the strength and endurance self-assessment this week.
Log the results in the app.

recommendations.trigger: Strength (e.g. ARED 1RM or an isokinetic knee/ankle test) falls >10% below your personal baseline on 2 consecutive tests (derived threshold)
recommendations.action: Notify the crew medical officer to check adherence and nutrition and to adjust the exercise prescription on board.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

source.citation: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Evidence Report: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness (FINAL 03.04.2024)

steps: Send your strength results to the medical officer.
Review your exercise log and meals with them.

recommendations.trigger: Exercise adherence below plan for several days in a row (e.g. faulty equipment, illness, injury) – a prototype threshold
recommendations.action: Notify the medical officer for an alternative loading plan. Without heavy resistance exercise, bone loss rates approach the pre-ARED values (~1–1.5%/month).
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone

source.citation: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Evidence Report: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone (HRP-F07-ERFT.R2, 18.07.2024)

steps: Tell the medical officer why you missed sessions.
Agree on an alternative loading plan.

recommendations.trigger: Strength falls >20% below baseline (derived threshold), or the estimated cumulative BMD loss exceeds 10% at the hip or spine (threshold derived from the Bone Summit criterion)
recommendations.action: Contact the medical team on the ground (flight surgeon) to review the prescription and any further countermeasure. In one study, a drug countermeasure combined with ARED prevented the drop in hip BMD (Sibonga 2019), but that decision belongs to the doctors on Earth.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone

source.citation: Sibonga J, Matsumoto T, Jones J, Shapiro J, Lang T, Shackelford L, Smith SM, Young M, Keyak J, Kohri K, Ohshima H, Spector E, LeBlanc A (2019). Resistive exercise in astronauts on prolonged spaceflights provides partial protection against spaceflight-induced bone loss. Bone 128:112037

steps: Send your strength and exercise data to Earth.
Keep up your current prescription until you get an answer.

recommendations.trigger: Before a gravity transition (lunar landing, surface EVA, return to Earth) with large strength or bone deficits vs baseline
recommendations.action: Report to the ground: the risk of falls and fractures rises at gravity transitions, and the FOR (applied load / bone strength) increases when bone is weakened.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Mission Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness

source.citation: NASA HRP (2025). Risk of Reduced Cardiorespiratory and Musculoskeletal Fitness (official page, updated 16 May 2025)

steps: Report your strength and bone estimates to the ground.
Plan the transition with support from a crewmate.

recommendations.trigger: After the mission (especially >6 months): planning the follow-up
recommendations.action: Recommend QCT/HR-pQCT follow-up, not just DXA. Trabecular bone recovery can be incomplete at 1–2 years, even when DXA shows a return to normal.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone

source.citation: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Evidence Report: Risk of Bone Fracture due to Spaceflight-induced Changes to Bone (HRP-F07-ERFT.R2, 18.07.2024)

steps: Book a QCT or HR-pQCT scan after the mission.
Keep up loaded exercise after landing.

recommendations.trigger: SEP alert: the habitat dose rate is ≥2× its 24-h average (derived threshold), or an SEP event notification from the ground.
recommendations.action: Go immediately to the most shielded area (the crew quarters surrounded by water containers / hydrogen-rich materials such as polyethylene) and stay there until the dose rate returns to baseline.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA. Space Radiation Won't Stop NASA's Human Exploration.

steps: Go immediately to the most shielded area.
Press “I'm in the shelter” in the app.
Stay there until the dose rate is back to normal.

recommendations.trigger: Vehicle beyond low Earth orbit, with an early SEP warning received before the particles arrive.
recommendations.action: Reconfigure the shelter: move the water containers and luggage bags around the crew quarters (target: +10 cm water equivalent); the SEP timeline usually leaves time to reconfigure.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (2025). NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 Rev G (06/06/2025): Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection.

steps: Move the water containers around the crew quarters.
Stack luggage bags along the walls.
Check that the shelter is ready before the particles arrive.

recommendations.trigger: SEP alert during an extravehicular activity (EVA).
recommendations.action: Stop the EVA and get back into the vehicle or behind shielding within 2 hours of the alert.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (2025). NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 Rev G (06/06/2025): Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection.

steps: Stop the EVA now.
Return to the vehicle or to shielding within 2 hours.

recommendations.trigger: An EVA is planned while an SEP is under way or a space weather alert is active.
recommendations.action: Postpone the EVA until the alert is over. The NASA brief says only that SEPs severely disrupt EVAs; the postponement rule is our extrapolation.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (2025). NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 Rev G (06/06/2025): Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection.

steps: Postpone the EVA.
Wait until the alert is over before going out.

recommendations.trigger: Always (routine monitoring).
recommendations.action: Wear your personal dosimeter at all times and apply the ALARA principle: during an alert, limit the time spent in poorly shielded modules.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA (2025/2026). NASA-STD-3001, NASA Space Flight Human-System Standard, Volume 1 Rev C: Crew Health, Section 4.8 Space Permissible Exposure Limit for Spaceflight Radiation Exposure [V1 4029-4031] (web version, page last updated Mar 18, 2026).

steps: Wear your dosimeter at all times.
During an alert, limit time in poorly shielded modules.

recommendations.trigger: After an SEP, the crew member has nausea, vomiting or unusual tiredness compared with their personal baseline.
recommendations.action: Notify the crew medical officer: these symptoms match acute radiation syndrome and must be correlated with the dose recorded by the dosimeter.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes and Decrements in Performance due to Inflight Medical Conditions (acute radiation syndrome as an in-mission risk, per OCHMO-TB-020)

source.citation: NASA Office of the Chief Health & Medical Officer (2025). NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-020 Rev G (06/06/2025): Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection.

steps: Tell the medical officer how you feel.
Check the dose recorded on your dosimeter.
Rest and drink fluids until you are assessed.

recommendations.trigger: The 30-day accumulated dose (personal dosimeter) exceeds 50% of NASA's 250 mGy-Eq limit for the blood-forming organs or the circulatory system (the 50% fraction is derived).
recommendations.action: The medical officer reviews the dose history, checks that sheltering was done correctly and plans to reduce exposure (ALARA) over the next days.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA (2025/2026). NASA-STD-3001, NASA Space Flight Human-System Standard, Volume 1 Rev C: Crew Health, Section 4.8 Space Permissible Exposure Limit for Spaceflight Radiation Exposure [V1 4029-4031] (web version, page last updated Mar 18, 2026).

steps: Share your dosimeter history with the medical officer.
Follow the exposure plan for the next days.

recommendations.trigger: The dose accumulated since the start of the SEP is ≥ 25 mGy-Eq (10% of the 30-day limit for the blood-forming organs; derived threshold), or the projected career dose exceeds 600 mSv.
recommendations.action: Send a report to Earth (dose, duration, shelter location). On Mars the answer comes ~6–45 min round trip at the earliest, so the decision to shelter does not wait for it.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers (formal: Risk of Radiation Carcinogenesis)

source.citation: NASA (2025/2026). NASA-STD-3001, NASA Space Flight Human-System Standard, Volume 1 Rev C: Crew Health, Section 4.8 Space Permissible Exposure Limit for Spaceflight Radiation Exposure [V1 4029-4031] (web version, page last updated Mar 18, 2026).

steps: Send the dose report to Earth.
Stay in the shelter; don't wait for the reply.

recommendations.trigger: An estimated whole-body dose approaching 0.7 Gy within a short time, or symptoms of acute radiation syndrome.
recommendations.action: Medical emergency: notify Earth (the flight surgeon) immediately and follow the on-board medical protocol without waiting for an answer, because of the delay.
recommendations.hrp_risk: Risk of Adverse Health Outcomes and Decrements in Performance due to Inflight Medical Conditions

source.citation: Guo J., Zeitlin C., Wimmer-Schweingruber R.F., Hassler D.M., Ehresmann B., Rafkin S., Freiherr von Forstner J.L., Khaksarighiri S., Liu W., Wang Y. (2021). Radiation environment for future human exploration on the surface of Mars: the current understanding based on MSL/RAD dose measurements. The Astronomy and Astrophysics Review 29: 8.

steps: Alert the medical officer and Earth now.
Follow the on-board medical protocol.
Don't wait for an answer from Earth.
